title: Whole Smoked Gator
finish: 160°F in the tail and the thickest part of the rear legs
summary: A whole Mississippi gator on the grate. Tail stuffed with store-bought boudin, pecan smoke, cayenne butter.
story: A whole gator on a pit is a Delta party, not a weeknight. Farm-raised, already gutted, 15–30 pounds is what a backyard offset or a big kettle can hold. Inject the tail and rear legs for moisture — brine it too if you have a tub big enough to hold it — then butterfly the tail and pack it with store-bought boudin (boudan) — the grocery links, not a from-scratch sausage project. Pecan wood, 250°F, 160°F in the tail. The boudin comes out as a dirty-rice stuffing in the tail. Lemon and hot sauce on the table.

items: 1 whole alligator, 15–30 lb, gutted, cleaned, and skinned (farm-raised)
Skin off so the rub sticks. Ask the processor to skin it for you if you don't want that job.
1½–2 lb store-bought Cajun boudin links (pork and rice — the grocery case, not homemade)
1–2 cups of that brine, cooled, for injecting the tail and rear legs

steps.title: Skin, clean, butterfly the tail
steps.body:
Gator should come gutted and skinned. The rub needs meat, not armor.
Rinse the cavity. Pat dry.
From the underside, butterfly the thick tail — a long cut down the middle, not all the way through, so you have a pocket for the boudin.
If it's too long for your pit, take the tail off and run it beside the body. Same recipe.

steps.title: Inject and brine
steps.body:
Stir salt and sugar into the water. Add hot sauce and garlic. Cool it.
Inject the tail and both rear legs in a grid — gator is lean, same idea as venison, and that injection is what keeps it moist.
Then brine it if you can find a tub big enough to just leave it brining in — I cook mine whole. A lot of folks cut it up so it fits a tub, and that works too. If you can't brine at all, the injection alone carries the moisture.

steps.title: Stuff the tail with boudin
steps.body:
After the brine: rinse and pat dry — if you skipped the soak and only injected, just pat dry.
Turn the gator tail-up. From the underside, butterfly the thick tail — a long cut down the middle, not all the way through, so you have a pocket.
Squeeze the boudin out of the casings (or nestle whole links if that's easier). Pack it in. Don't overfill or it blows out on the pit.
Tie the tail shut with butcher twine every couple of inches. Most store boudin is already cooked. You're heating it with the gator, not making sausage.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Cavity, legs, stuffed tail — paprika, salt, cayenne, garlic, onion, pepper, thyme. Skinless meat will take a heavy coat. That's what you want.

steps.title: Pecan, 250–275°F
steps.body:
You need grate space. Belly down or on its side, tail toward the cooler end of the pit if you have one.
Pecan if you have it, hickory if you don't. Thin blue smoke.
A 20-pound gator is often 6–8 hours. Bigger takes longer.
Probe the thickest tail meat and a rear leg. Both need 160°F. The thin body will get there first — mop it so it doesn't turn to jerky.

steps.title: Butter mop, rest, pick
steps.body:
Last 30 minutes, brush melted butter mixed with lemon juice on the tail, legs, and any exposed meat.
Rest 20–30 minutes.
Cut the twine. Slice the tail across — you should get a round of gator with a boudin center, like a stuffed loin.
Legs next. Body meat is for hash or gumbo if it's dry.
Lemon, hot sauce, white bread. 160°F in the tail meat, not in the rice.

proTips.text: Call a processor or a Gulf farm. A whole wild gator on a backyard pit is a permitting problem, not a recipe. Farm-raised, gutted, 15–30 lb is the cook.
If it won't fit, stuff and smoke the tail with the boudin and run the rear legs beside it. Don't fold a 6-foot gator into a kettle and call it done.

milestones.label: Injected and brined
milestones.hint: Tail and rear legs. Overnight if you can.

milestones.label: Tail stuffed
milestones.hint: Butterfly, pack store boudin, tie it.

milestones.label: Rubbed
milestones.hint: Cavity, legs, tail. Skinless meat takes a heavy coat.

milestones.label: 160°F tail and leg
milestones.hint: Pecan, 250–275°F. Mop the thin parts.

milestones.label: Rested and picked
milestones.hint: Tail first. Butter mop. Lemon and hot sauce.

title: Florida Sweet Ribs
finish: Bend test, then a late orange-sweet glaze
summary: Spare ribs, a brown-sugar rub, Florida sweet sauce with orange juice. Shiny on purpose.
story: North Florida ribs are supposed to be sweet. Not a dry Texas crust. You smoke them until they bend, then glaze with ketchup, brown sugar, and orange juice so they shine. If you want them drier, you're in the wrong state. White bread, pickles, extra sauce on the table.

items: 2 racks spare ribs, St. Louis cut
1 cup Florida Sweet Sauce (the recipe in this app), or
¾ cup ketchup + ¼ cup orange juice + 2 Tbsp honey + 1 Tbsp brown sugar, warmed

steps.title: Peel the membrane
steps.body: Bone side. Loosen with a knife, pull with a paper towel. Leave it and the bite is leather.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body:
Thin mustard. Brown-sugar rub, heavier on the meat side.
Rest 30 minutes while the pit comes to 250–275°F.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body:
Pecan, apple, or orange wood. Bone-side down. 4–5 hours.
Spritz with orange juice or apple juice if they look dry after 90 minutes.
Don't wrap unless you're late for dinner.

steps.title: Glaze late
steps.body:
When they bend and the meat has pulled back about ¼ inch, brush a thin coat of Florida sweet sauce.
15–20 minutes. Another thin coat. Sugar burns if you sauce them at hour two.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes. Slice between the bones. Extra sauce on the table. That's Florida.

proTips.text: The orange is the difference between this and Kansas City. Don't skip it and just use a grocery bottle of KC sauce.

milestones.label: Rubbed
milestones.hint: Membrane off. Brown sugar rub.

milestones.label: Bend test
milestones.hint: 4–5 hours. ¼ inch pullback.

milestones.label: Glazed
milestones.hint: Two thin coats. Last 20 minutes.

title: Mississippi Sweet Ribs
finish: Bend test, then a dark molasses glaze
summary: Delta wet ribs. Hickory, a sweet rub, Mississippi tomato-molasses sauce mopped on late. Darker and stickier than Florida.
story: Mississippi likes ribs wet and sweet — molasses in the bottle, hickory in the fire, a shine on the bone. Closer to Memphis wet than to Texas. You smoke them until they bend, then mop on that dark red sauce so they come off looking like candy and tasting like pork. Extra sauce on the table is not optional.

items: 2 racks spare ribs, St. Louis cut
1 cup Mississippi Sweet Sauce (the recipe in this app), or
¾ cup ketchup + 2 Tbsp molasses + 2 Tbsp brown sugar + 1 Tbsp cider vinegar, warmed

steps.title: Peel the membrane
steps.body: Bone side. Knife, paper towel, pull. Same as every other rack in this app.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body:
Thin mustard. Rub both sides, heavier on the meat.
Rest 30 minutes. Pit at 250–275°F.

steps.title: Hickory smoke
steps.body:
Bone-side down. Hickory. 4–5 hours.
Spritz with apple juice if they look dry.
Unwrapped unless dinner is waiting.

steps.title: Wet glaze
steps.body:
When they bend, mop on Mississippi sweet sauce. Thin coat. 15 minutes. Another coat.
They should look wet and dark, not dry-dusted. That's the Delta.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes. Slice between bones. Bottle of sauce on the table. White bread.

proTips.text: Florida is orange-sweet. Mississippi is molasses-sweet. Don't swap the bottles and tell people it's all the same South.

milestones.label: Rubbed
milestones.hint: Membrane off. Brown sugar and paprika.

milestones.label: Bend test
milestones.hint: Hickory, 4–5 hours.

milestones.label: Wet and dark
milestones.hint: Two thin molasses coats. Last 20 minutes.

title: Copycat P.F. Chang's Spare Ribs
finish: Sticky dark glaze, meat pulling from the bone, sesame and scallion on top
summary: A copycat of P.F. Chang's Chinese spare ribs. Hoisin, soy, honey, garlic. Smoke first, glaze late.
story: The restaurant ribs are sweet, salty, and sticky — hoisin and honey more than barbecue sauce. This is a home copycat for the pit: fruit wood until the rack bends, then a hoisin-soy-honey glaze so they shine like the plate you remember. Not Kansas City. Not Carolina. Sesame seeds and green onion at the end. White rice if you want the full booth.

items: 2 racks spare ribs or baby backs, membrane off

steps.title: Season the racks
steps.body:
Peel the membrane off the bone side.
Salt, five-spice, and black pepper — a light coat, not a Texas crust.
Rest 20 minutes while you light 250–275°F.

steps.title: Make the glaze
steps.body:
Hoisin, honey, soy, rice vinegar, brown sugar, ketchup, garlic, ginger, sesame oil, five-spice, and pepper flakes in a saucepan.
Low heat 8–10 minutes until it looks shiny and thick enough to coat a spoon.
Pull ⅓ cup off for the table. The rest is for the pit.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body:
Apple or cherry wood. Bone-side down.
Baby backs 3–3½ hours. Spareribs 4–4½ hours.
Done when they bend and the meat has pulled back about ¼ inch.
Don't sauce them yet.

steps.title: Glaze late
steps.body:
Brush a thin coat of glaze. 10 minutes.
Another thin coat. 10 minutes.
Sugar burns if you start this at hour one. Shine comes from two late coats, not a puddle.

steps.title: Rest and cut
steps.body:
Rest 10 minutes.
Slice between the bones.
Sesame seeds and green onion on top. Warm glaze on the table.
Rice and a cucumber salad if you want the restaurant plate.

proTips.text: This is a home version of the flavor, not the restaurant's kitchen formula. Hoisin is the body. If you swap in Kansas City sauce you made a different rib.
No pit: 300°F on a rack over a pan, foil 2 hours, uncover, glaze, 15 minutes more. Same bottle of glaze.

milestones.label: Glaze simmered
milestones.hint: Hoisin, honey, soy. Shiny, coats a spoon.

milestones.label: Bend test
milestones.hint: Apple or cherry. Don't sauce yet.

milestones.label: Two late coats
milestones.hint: 10 minutes apart. Then sesame and scallion.

title: Smoked Meatloaf
finish: 160°F in the center, glaze set, slices hold together
summary: A free-form loaf on the grate. Smoke, then a late barbecue glaze. Weeknight meatloaf that tastes like it sat next to the ribs.
story: Meatloaf on a pit is just a hamburger that learned patience. Mix it so it holds, shape it on a rack so smoke can get under it, and leave the ketchup glaze for the last half hour so the sugar doesn't burn. Hickory or oak. 160°F in the middle. Slice thick. The leftovers make the sandwich that justifies the cook.

items: 2 lb ground beef (80/20), or 1½ lb beef + ½ lb ground pork
1 small onion, grated or minced fine
½ cup barbecue sauce (Kansas City style, or whatever's in the fridge)

steps.title: Mix, don't knead
steps.body:
Milk on the breadcrumbs. Sit 5 minutes so they soak.
Add the meat, onion, garlic, egg, Worcestershire, mustard, salt, pepper, paprika, thyme.
Hands. Mix just until it holds. If you work it like bread it eats like a brick.

steps.title: Shape on a rack
steps.body:
Free-form loaf about 9 inches long and 3 inches high, on a wire rack over a pan.
Don't pack it into a loaf tin — the smoke needs the sides.
A shallow groove down the middle keeps it from puffing into a meatball.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body:
250–275°F. Hickory or oak. Thin blue smoke.
Rack on the grate. Leave it alone.
Probe the center. You're waiting on about 145°F before you glaze — usually 2–2½ hours.

steps.title: Glaze and finish
steps.body:
Stir barbecue sauce, brown sugar, and vinegar.
Brush a thin coat. 15 minutes. Another coat.
Pull at 160°F in the center. Usually 30–45 minutes after the first glaze.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body:
Rest 15 minutes or it crumbles on the knife.
Slice thick. Extra sauce on the table.
Cold the next day on white bread with pickles is the real prize.

proTips.text: A loaf pan steams it. A rack smokes it. If you only have a pan, set the loaf on a small rack inside the pan so fat can drip.
Half pork makes it juicier. All beef is fine. Turkey meatloaf dries out on a pit unless you add a grated apple or extra fat.

milestones.label: Shaped on a rack
milestones.hint: Free-form. Don't pack a tin.

milestones.label: ~145°F
milestones.hint: Hickory or oak. Then glaze.

milestones.label: 160°F glazed
milestones.hint: Two thin coats. Rest 15 minutes.

title: Dry Rub Spare Ribs
finish: Bend test, spice crust, no sauce on the rack
summary: St. Louis–cut spares, a paprika dry rub, hickory. Sauce stays on the table. The crust is the point.
story: Dry-rub ribs are what you cook when you want pork and smoke and spice, not a candy glaze. Peel the membrane, coat them heavy, and leave them alone on hickory until they bend. A last dusting of rub while they're tacky is the whole trick. If you brush sauce on the rack you made wet ribs. That's a different cook — Florida and Mississippi already have those.

items: 2 racks spare ribs, St. Louis cut

ingredients.group: Dry rub (save 3 Tbsp for the finish)

steps.title: Peel the membrane
steps.body:
Bone side. Loosen with a knife, pull with a paper towel.
Leave it and the rub never gets through.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body:
Thin mustard on both sides.
Coat with the rub — heavier on the meat side. Keep 3 tablespoons in a cup for the end.
Rest 30 minutes while the pit comes to 250–275°F.

steps.title: Hickory, no wrap
steps.body:
Bone-side down. Hickory. Thin blue smoke.
4½–5½ hours. Spritz with a little apple cider vinegar only if the rub looks powdery and dry.
Do not wrap. Do not sauce.

steps.title: Bend, then dust
steps.body:
Pick up the rack with tongs in the middle. It should bend into a U and crack on top, not break in half.
Meat pulled back about ¼ inch from the bone.
Dust the reserved rub on while the surface is still tacky.
Rest 10 minutes. Slice between the bones. Sauce on the table if somebody asks.

proTips.text: The second rub is not optional. Without it you have smoked pork. With it you have a crust.
Baby backs are the other dry-rib cook in this app (Memphis Dry Ribs) — faster, leaner. These spares take the longer fire and feed more people.

milestones.label: Rubbed
milestones.hint: Membrane off. Save 3 Tbsp for the finish.

milestones.label: Bend test
milestones.hint: Hickory, no wrap, no sauce.

milestones.label: Finish dust
milestones.hint: Reserved rub on tacky bark. Rest 10.

title: Championship Pulled Pork
finish: Probe tender, 200–205°F, pulls with no fight
summary: Championship-circuit pulled pork: inject, smoke, wrap with brown sugar, honey, and butter, then pull.
story: Circuit pork is not Eastern Carolina vinegar hog. You inject the butt so it stays juicy, build a sweet bark, then wrap it in foil with brown sugar, honey, and butter until a probe slides like butter. Pull it, toss it with the wrap juice, a little sauce. Soft buns.

items: ½–1 cup sweet barbecue sauce (Kansas City style, or Mississippi Sweet Sauce from this app)

steps.title: Inject
steps.body:
Stir the injection until the sugar dissolves.
Inject the butt in a grid — top, sides, around the bone. Use most of it.
Pat dry. The juice is insurance for a leaner shoulder.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body:
Coat every side with the rub. Don't be shy — championship pork is mahogany, not shy pink.
Rest 30 minutes while you light 250–275°F. Hickory or pecan.

steps.title: Smoke for bark
steps.body:
Fat-cap up. Leave it alone 5–6 hours, until the bark is set and the internal is around 165–170°F.
Don't wrap early. The bark has to exist before the foil or you steamed a roast.

steps.title: The money wrap
steps.body:
Heavy-duty foil. Brown sugar, honey, and butter on the foil. Butt on top, fat-cap up.
More brown sugar and a few dots of butter on the cap.
Wrap tight. Back on the pit at 250–275°F until a probe slides like warm butter, 200–205°F — usually 3–4 more hours.

steps.title: Rest, pull, gloss
steps.body:
Rest in the wrap 45–60 minutes.
Pour the wrap juice into a bowl. Skim the grease if it's a pond.
Pull the pork. Discard bone and big gristle. Toss with enough juice to shine, then a little sweet sauce — gloss, not soup.
Buns, slaw. This is not vinegar Carolina. Don't pretend it is.

proTips.text: Inject, bark, then a sweet wrap. That's the circuit method. A boxed rub from the store is fine if you already like one.
Foil, not butcher paper. Paper is for brisket bark. This wrap is a braise on purpose. That's how championship pork stays wet in a box.

milestones.label: Injected
milestones.hint: Apple juice grid. Then the rub.

milestones.label: Bark set
milestones.hint: 165–170°F. Mahogany. Then wrap.

milestones.label: Money wrap
milestones.hint: Brown sugar, honey, butter. Tight foil.

milestones.label: Probe and pull
milestones.hint: 200–205°F. Rest in the wrap. Gloss, don't drown.

title: Championship Chili
pitTemp: Smoke the beef at 250°F, then a low simmer
finish: Thick red gravy, beans tender, beef in cubes not mush
summary: Competition homestyle chili with beans. Smoked chuck, Hatch chiles, pinto beans, real chile — not a packet.
story: ICS Texas Red does not allow beans. Homestyle does, and homestyle is what people actually eat. This is the cup that wins a backyard cook-off: smoked chuck for the chew, a little hot sausage for fat, roasted Hatch chiles, two kinds of chile powder, beer, cocoa, and pinto beans that hold their shape. Build it in layers. Don't dump everything in a pot and hope. Serve with Fritos, cheddar, onion. The next day is better.

items: 3 lb beef chuck, cut in ½-inch cubes
2–3 Hatch green chiles, roasted, peeled, seeded, chopped (3 if you want it louder)
1 jalapeño, minced (seeds if you want heat)
2 (15 oz) cans pinto beans, drained and rinsed
2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

steps.title: Smoke the chuck
steps.body:
Salt the cubes. 250°F, post oak or hickory, about 1 hour — just enough for smoke, not until they're pot roast.
They finish in the pot.

steps.title: Brown
steps.body:
Dutch oven on the pit or the stove.
Bacon first. Pull it.
Sausage in the fat, break it up, brown it, pull it.
Chuck cubes in batches so they sear, not steam. Pull them.

steps.title: Build the gravy
steps.body:
Onion, bell pepper, Hatch chiles, and jalapeño in the pot. 5 minutes until soft.
Garlic 30 seconds. Tomato paste 1 minute until it darkens.
Spice in. Stir 30 seconds so the chile toasts.
Crushed tomatoes, tomato sauce, broth, beer. Scrape the brown off the bottom.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Beef, sausage, and bacon back in.
Low simmer, lid cracked, 2–2½ hours until the chuck is tender and the gravy is thick.
Stir so it doesn't stick.

steps.title: Beans last
steps.body:
Pinto beans in for the last 20–30 minutes. They should hold their shape, not dissolve.
Taste. Salt. A pinch more cayenne if it's shy. A pinch more brown sugar if the tomatoes are sharp.
Rest 15 minutes off the heat.

proTips.text: Beans go in late. Two hours of simmer turns them to paste and the judges notice.
Two Hatch chiles is friendly. Three is noticeable. Hatch season is late summer. Off-season, a small can or frozen roasted Hatch is the honest swap.

milestones.label: Chuck smoked
milestones.hint: 1 hour at 250°F. Then the pot.

milestones.label: Tender beef
milestones.hint: 2–2½ hours. Gravy thick.

milestones.label: Beans in
milestones.hint: Last 20–30 minutes. Then rest.

title: Kentucky Burgoo
pitTemp: Smoke the meats, then a long simmer
finish: Thick stew. A spoon should stand a second, then fall.
summary: Owensboro picnic stew. Mutton if you can get it, deer if you choose, chicken, pork, corn, lima beans, potatoes.
story: Burgoo is what Kentucky puts on a paper plate next to chopped mutton. Moonlite and Old Hickory sell it by the gallon. The honest pot is mixed meat — mutton for the wool-and-Worcestershire taste, chicken for broth, a little pork for fat — then corn, lima beans, potato, and enough black dip that it tastes like Western Kentucky, not vegetable soup. No mutton at the shop — extra pork shoulder, or deer stew meat if that's what's in the freezer. Venison is lean; inject it with a little beef broth before the smoke so the pot stays wet.

items: 2 lb mutton or lamb stew meat — or 2 lb deer stew meat if you choose (pork shoulder if you have neither)

steps.title: Smoke the meats
steps.body:
Salt the mutton, lamb, or deer, plus the pork and chicken.
If you're using deer, inject a little beef broth first — venison is lean and the pot needs that moisture.
Hickory, 250°F, about 1½ hours — smoke on them, not cooked through.
They finish in the pot.

steps.title: Start the pot
steps.body:
Oil in a heavy pot. Onion, carrot, celery, bell pepper 6–8 minutes.
Garlic 30 seconds.
Meats in. Broth, tomatoes, Worcestershire, vinegar, salt, pepper, paprika, cayenne, bay.
Bring to a simmer.

steps.title: Long and low
steps.body:
Lid cracked. 3–4 hours, stirring now and then, until the meats shred when you poke them.
Pull the chicken bones and bay leaves. Shred big pieces back into the pot.

steps.title: Vegetables
steps.body:
Potatoes in. 20 minutes.
Lima beans, corn, okra in. 20–30 minutes more until the potatoes are soft and the stew is thick.
If it's soup, keep the lid off and let it reduce. Burgoo is not broth.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
More Worcestershire if it tastes like stew from nowhere.
More vinegar if it's dull.
Salt last.
Rest 15 minutes. Cornbread or saltines. Chopped mutton on the side if you smoked a shoulder.

proTips.text: Lamb is younger and milder. Mutton is the Owensboro taste. Deer is a Kentucky freezer swap — same weight, inject beef broth because it's lean, keep the pork in the pot for fat. Pork shoulder plus extra Worcestershire if you have neither sheep nor deer.
Some pots mash a few potatoes against the side to thicken. Don't add flour. This isn't gravy.

milestones.label: Meats smoked
milestones.hint: Hickory, 1½ hours. Then the pot.

milestones.label: Meat shreds
milestones.hint: 3–4 hours. Bones out.

milestones.label: Thick
milestones.hint: Potatoes, lima, corn. Spoon stands.

title: Championship Pork Injection
servings: Enough for two 8–10 lb Boston butts
finish: Clear amber. Sugar and salt dissolved. No grit in the needle.
summary: Apple juice, water, sugar, salt, Worcestershire, soy. A championship shot for a Boston butt.
story: Circuit pork gets a shot before it hits the pit — a quick brine in the muscle so an 8-pound butt doesn't dry out. Apple juice, white sugar and brown sugar, enough salt that it seasons from the inside, Worcestershire and soy for the middle. Stir until nothing sits on the bottom or you'll clog the needle. Grid the butt. Don't dump it in a bowl and call it a marinade.

items: ¼ cup packed dark brown sugar

steps.title: Dissolve
steps.body:
Warm the apple juice and water just enough that both sugars and the salt disappear. Don't boil.
Worcestershire, soy, vinegar.
Cool until you can touch it. Hot injection cooks the meat from the inside.

steps.title: Strain
steps.body:
Pour through a mesh strainer or coffee filter if any grit remains.
A clogged needle is a ruined Saturday.

steps.title: Grid the butt
steps.body:
Injector, 1-inch squares, top and sides, around the bone.
Go in, inject, change the angle without pulling all the way out, inject again.
Use most of the cup on one 8–10 lb butt. This batch covers two.

steps.title: Rub and rest
steps.body:
Pat the surface dry. Rub. Rest 30 minutes while the pit comes up.
Then smoke like Championship Pulled Pork or any Boston butt in this app.

proTips.text: White sugar and brown sugar both go in the cup. All brown works. All white works. Don't add rub — it clogs the needle.
Kosher salt. Table salt at this volume will oversalt. If all you have is table salt, use 2 tablespoons, not a quarter cup.

milestones.label: Dissolved
milestones.hint: No grit. Cool to the touch.

milestones.label: Gridded
milestones.hint: 1-inch squares. Then the rub.

title: Santa Maria Seasoning
finish: Salty, garlicky, green flecks of parsley
summary: Salt, garlic, pepper, parsley. The Central Coast ranch rub that belongs on tri-tip, not a 14-hour packer.
story: Santa Maria barbecue is live oak and a beef roast, not a molasses bottle. The seasoning is almost a steak rub: plenty of granulated garlic, salt, coarse pepper, and dried parsley. Rosemary if you want the old pinquito-bean supper. Put it on tri-tip, a ribeye, or chicken over coals. It is too loud for a Central Texas brisket and too simple for competition pork.

steps.title: Whisk dry
steps.body: Garlic should be granulated, not garlic salt — you already measured salt. Parsley is color and a little herb, not a garnish after the fact.

steps.title: On the meat
steps.body: A hard coat on tri-tip 30 minutes before the fire. For steaks, 10 minutes so the salt doesn't draw too much juice. Sear, then finish indirect.

proTips.text: The wood is red oak. The seasoning is garlic. If you skip either, you just grilled a roast.

milestones.label: Mix
milestones.hint: Salt, garlic, pepper, parsley.

milestones.label: Jar
milestones.hint: Use on tri-tip the same week you grind the garlic smell into the kitchen.

title: Memphis Dry Rub
summary: Paprika, thyme, mustard, a little brown sugar. The crust you dust on twice — once before the fire, once at the end.
story: Memphis dry is a spice crust, not a sauce failure. Paprika for color, brown sugar in a supporting role, thyme and mustard so it smells like a spice house instead of a rib shack candle. Save a few tablespoons to dust the rack when it comes off, while the surface is still tacky.

steps.title: Whisk until even
steps.body: Break up the brown sugar first. The mix should be brick-red with visible thyme, not a brown paste.

steps.title: Two coats
steps.body: Binder of oil or mustard, then a coat before the pit. Dust again when the ribs come off. Sauce stays in a cup on the table.

proTips.text: If you need a wet glaze to make this taste like something, you put it on too light or you cooked the ribs to mush.

milestones.label: Mix
milestones.hint: Brick-red, no sugar lumps.

milestones.label: Second dust
milestones.hint: On the tacky rack, off the pit.

title: Cajun Pit Rub
finish: Rusty red, thyme in the nose, heat in the finish
summary: Paprika, cayenne, thyme, oregano, garlic. The Louisiana coat for turkey, sausage, and a pork shoulder that wants to argue.
story: Cajun seasoning on a smoker is not blackening in a screaming skillet. You still want salt and paprika as the body, cayenne as a line, and the herbal note that says this came from a Louisiana cabinet. Good on a spatchcock turkey, hot links, and a picnic ham. Easy to overdo on a 12-hour brisket — the cayenne will taste like a dare by hour ten.

items: 1 Tbsp cayenne (use 2 tsp if you are polite)

steps.title: Mix and smell
steps.body: If you cannot smell thyme, add a pinch more. If it only smells like heat, you dumped too much cayenne.

steps.title: Where it belongs
steps.body: Turkey, chicken, pork shoulder, sausage. A dusting on shrimp for a two-zone grill. Not a substitute for Dalmatian on beef ribs.

proTips.text: White pepper is the quiet heat people cannot name. Skip it and the rub tastes like chili powder from a packet.

milestones.label: Mix
milestones.hint: Thyme in the nose, cayenne in the finish.

milestones.label: Jar
milestones.hint: Label it. You will grab this instead of paprika at 6 a.m.
